questions.q: A writer's sixty-page second act sags. What does the sequence approach suggest?
choices: Break it into about four sequences, each with its own goal and tension
Move the crisis into Act I
questions.explain: Two sequences in Act I, four in Act II, two in Act III makes the middle manageable.

questions.q: What makes a sequence more than just a stretch of pages?
choices: It has its own goal, its own tension and a resolution, like a short film
It's always set in a single location
It must end on a cliffhanger
questions.explain: Each sequence poses and answers its own question, usually launching the next one.

questions.q: What's the best way to treat the number eight?
choices: As an industry rule written into contracts
As Aristotle's original division of tragedy
As a typical pattern for a two-hour film, which can vary
As the number of acts in a feature
questions.explain: Gulino doesn't treat eight as a law; some films have fewer or more sequences.

questions.q: According to this school of teaching, tension in the audience is built from what?
questions.explain: The audience hopes for one outcome and fears another. Pity and fear are Aristotle's tragic emotions.

questions.q: What is the 'main tension' of a film?
choices: The overarching dramatic question, usually set up by the end of Act I
The tension of the final sequence only
The conflict between the writer and the studio
questions.explain: The sequences work toward answering it, while each poses smaller questions of its own.

questions.q: Why is Frank Daniel's approach known mainly through other people's books?
choices: He taught it in classrooms and didn't publish a screenwriting book of his own
questions.explain: Students and colleagues such as Paul Gulino and David Howard set out his ideas in print.

questions.q: An audience knows a bomb is under the table, but the characters don't. Which tool is that?
questions.explain: Dramatic irony, the audience knowing more than a character, is one of the tools the sequence approach uses to build tension.

ideas: A feature film is a chain of roughly eight short films, each 10 to 15 minutes long with its own tension.
Each sequence needs its own goal, its own question and its own resolution, which launches the next.
Tension is built from hope and fear: the audience hopes for one outcome and dreads another.
